title: Immigration Cannot Solve the US Birth Dearth
author: Camarota, Steven A.
summary: Steven Camarota argues that while immigrant women have slightly higher fertility rates (2.19 vs. 1.73 for native-born), immigration cannot meaningfully address America's fertility crisis. Immigrants age over time and their fertility patterns converge with native-born populations, producing only marginal demographic impact. Higher immigration may actually create housing and economic pressure that reduces native-born fertility. The analysis suggests that immigration alone cannot reverse the deeper cultural and economic forces driving sustained low fertility across the population.
points: Immigrant women have higher fertility rates (2.19) but combining with native-born (1.73) raises overall rate only from 1.73 to 1.80—a marginal 4.5 percent increase.
Immigrants are not all young women having large families; many are older and their fertility patterns quickly converge with native-born populations.
Higher immigration creates housing and economic pressures that may reduce fertility among the native-born population.
Immigration can slow population decline at margins but does not reverse deeper cultural and economic forces driving low fertility.
The fertility crisis reflects fundamental shifts in cultural values and economic incentives that immigration policy alone cannot address.
quotes: There is a growing naive assumption that immigration can solve America's fertility crisis. The data says otherwise.
Immigrants do not remain a permanently high-fertility group.
There is also evidence that higher immigration can put pressure on housing and economic conditions in ways that may reduce fertility among the native-born.
Immigration can slow population decline at the margins, but it does not reverse the deeper cultural and economic forces driving low fertility.” Archived from The Tennessee Star on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
